articles.author: ops-sd
articles.description:
Industrial maintenance teams still build machine-specific Lockout/Tagout (LOTO) placards in Word or PowerPoint, manually dragging red arrows onto shop-floor photos and hoping nothing shifts when printed at 11×17.
When we built LotoCard and the free .lotocard.json Field-Presence Viewer, our core engineering constraint was strict browser-local privacy: plant floor photos often contain proprietary tooling and layouts that EHS managers cannot upload to third-party cloud storage.
All machine photos, numbered energy-isolation callout pins (E-1, P-1, H-1), and revision metadata live in browser memory and serialize to a portable .lotocard.json document:
Photos are read via FileReader / ObjectURL, downscaled locally if needed, and never leave the browser tab.
Callout coordinates are stored as normalized [0..1] percentages relative to the image bounds so pins never drift between screen preview, 8.5×11 Letter, and 11×17 Tabloid PDFs.
OSHA 29 CFR 1910.147(c)(4)(ii) outlines specific procedural elements a machine-specific energy control procedure must document: intended use, shutdown steps, isolation devices, lockout/tagout application, stored energy dissipation, and verification of isolation.
Rather than claiming legal compliance certification, we modeled these as a deterministic field-presence completeness schema—highlighting missing verification steps or unpinned energy sources before a placard is printed and laminated.
Generating print-ready 8.5×11 and 11×17 placards directly in the browser with crisp vector callouts, OSHA-style hazard headers, and embedded QR revision codes avoids server-side Puppeteer cold starts and guarantees zero image upload.
If you want to inspect .lotocard.json files or test field-presence checks on 16 industrial machine presets (CNC mills, hydraulic presses, air compressors), try the free viewer at lotocards.com/loto-viewer.
articles.title: Building a 100% Browser-Local OSHA 1910.147 LOTO Placard Generator with Vector PDF Export

articles.author: zhangly1403
articles.description:
Standard web glTF/OBJ viewers usually run out of memory or stall for minutes when given multi-gigabyte industrial or BIM assemblies. I built and open-sourced 3dbrowser (GPL-3.0) to keep browser memory bounded and render the first frame quickly.
GitHub: https://github.com/zly258/3dbrowser


Tech Stack: React 19, Three.js, TypeScript, WebAssembly (web-ifc, occt-import-js)
When a 2+ GB BIM or plant assembly is exported to plain glTF/JSON, parsing and expanding it in the browser easily multiplies memory usage several times over, crashing the tab. Even if it fits in memory, hundreds of thousands of separate meshes produce too many WebGL draw calls.
3dbrowser is designed around six-figure component counts from the ground up:
NBIM v11 Single-File Container: Packs geometry, properties, and the structure tree into one binary container (with fixed-point coordinate quantization and columnar blocks).
Octree Chunk Streaming: Instead of waiting for the entire file to download before rendering, chunks stream in by spatial octree so the first frame appears in ~3–4.5s.
Three.js BatchedMesh: Merges heterogeneous components sharing materials into far fewer draw calls to maintain smooth frame rates.
On-Demand Property Resolution: Component metadata is resolved when selected rather than kept resident in memory alongside geometry.
Tested on a 2.9 GB NBIM file (231,353 components, 186 million rendered triangles) in a single browser tab while keeping JS heap under ~3 GB.
Supports IFC (web-ifc), STEP/STP & IGES/IGS (occt-import-js), GLB/GLTF, FBX, OBJ, STL, PLY, 3DS, DAE, and NBIM v11 (.nbim).
Includes distance/angle/point measurement, real-time sectioning planes, hierarchical scene tree search, and marquee box selection.
Multi-GB models need to be converted to the NBIM v11 format first; loading raw multi-GB IFC or STEP files directly in-browser is still bound by client-side WASM memory.
Licensed under GPL-3.0.
If you are working on WebGL CAD/BIM viewers or Three.js BatchedMesh pipelines, I'd love your feedback on the repo!
articles.title: 3dbrowser: Streaming a 2.9GB / 186M-Triangle BIM Model in Three.js Under ~3GB JS Heap

articles.description:
Originally published at SQL & Cloud Lab.
This post was drafted with AI assistance.
In the cloud, short interruptions are normal. Azure SQL Database occasionally moves a database to another node for maintenance, scaling or load balancing, and during those few seconds connections drop or new ones are refused. A well-built application shrugs these off with a short retry. A badly built one shows users an error page.

Only transient errors should be retried: ones that will probably succeed if you try again in a moment. Examples commonly treated as transient for Azure SQL include:
40613: database is not currently available (often during a failover).
40197: the service encountered an error processing your request.
40501: the service is currently busy.
49918, 49919, 49920: cannot process request b…
articles.title: Retry Logic for Azure SQL in .NET: Handling Transient Errors the Right Way
